hints: Focus on how Period 3 chlorides behave with water, silicon tetrachloride hydrolyses very readily.
Write the hydrolysis equation: $\text{SiCl}_4$ reacts to form solid silicon dioxide and hydrogen chloride gas.
Think about what you would actually see for each product, one gives a white solid in water and the other gives acidic mist in damp air.
walkthrough:
**Recall hydrolysis of covalent chlorides**

Think of $\text{SiCl}_4$ as a covalent, tetrahedral chloride that is readily attacked by water. Unlike $\text{CCl}_4$, silicon can expand its octet so hydrolysis is fast and vigorous.

Reaction type:
$$\text{chloride + water} \rightarrow \text{oxide + hydrogen chloride}$$

**Write the balanced equation**

Silicon forms silicon(IV) oxide and all four chlorides become $\text{HCl}$.

$$\text{SiCl}_4(l) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{SiO}_2(s) + 4\text{HCl}(g)$$

**Translate products into observations**

$\text{SiO}_2$ is an insoluble white solid, so you see a white precipitate in the beaker. $\text{HCl}$ gas mixes with moist air to form tiny droplets of hydrochloric acid, seen as dense white steamy fumes. Both are seen together.

options.A: Incorrect. No change would fit $\text{CCl}_4$, which does not hydrolyse, but $\text{SiCl}_4$ hydrolyses vigorously with water.
options.B: Correct. Hydrolysis gives $\text{SiO}_2(s)$ as a white precipitate and $\text{HCl}(g)$ which is observed as steamy white fumes in damp air.
options.C: Incorrect. A white precipitate of $\text{SiO}_2$ does form, but this misses the second product. The $\text{HCl}$ produced also gives very obvious steamy fumes.
options.D: Incorrect. Steamy fumes of $\text{HCl}$ are indeed seen, but this misses the second product. Insoluble $\text{SiO}_2$ also forms as a white precipitate.
